content: Autogenic drainage is a specialized airway clearance technique that was developed by Jean Chevaillier in 1967. This method involves controlled breathing to mobilize mucus from the smaller airways to the larger airways, allowing for independent clearance of secretions. The technique requires the individual to adjust the depth and speed of their breathing during exhalation in a structured sequence. While it demands significant training, focus, and effort, autogenic drainage has been shown to be an effective option for individuals seeking greater independence in managing their condition. However, given the evolving nature of cystic fibrosis and its treatment landscape, it is essential to systematically evaluate the evidence supporting the efficacy of autogenic drainage. The primary objective of this review was to compare the clinical effectiveness of autogenic drainage with other physiotherapy-based airway clearance techniques in individuals with cystic fibrosis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, which includes data from electronic databases, hand-searched journals, and conference abstracts. Additional searches were performed in reference lists of relevant articles and ongoing trial registries. The most recent search of the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register was conducted on July 6, 2021. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled studies that compared autogenic drainage to other airway clearance techniques or no therapy in individuals with cystic fibrosis. Studies were required to include at least two treatment sessions. Data extraction and risk of bias assessments were independently performed by three authors, and the quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE system. Seven research teams were contacted for additional information regarding their published studies. The search identified 64 references corresponding to 37 individual studies, of which eight studies (involving 212 participants) met the inclusion criteria. One study used a parallel design, while the remaining seven employed a cross-over design. The number of participants in each study ranged from 4 to 75, and the duration of the studies varied from four days to two years. Participants ranged in age from 7 to 63 years and exhibited a wide spectrum of disease severity. Six studies included clinically stable participants, while two studies involved individuals hospitalized for infective exacerbations. All studies compared autogenic drainage to one or more recognized airway clearance techniques. Notably, no studies were identified that compared autogenic drainage to exercise, which is commonly used as an alternative therapy by individuals with cystic fibrosis. The overall certainty of the evidence was rated as low or very low. This was primarily due to the frequent use of cross-over study designs, outcome reporting bias, and the inability to blind participants. The primary outcome of the review, forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), was the most commonly reported measure and was included in all eight studies. However, only three studies reported on quality of life, another primary outcome of the review. One study documented adverse events, noting a decrease in oxygen saturation levels during active cycle of breathing techniques but not during autogenic drainage. Seven studies measured forced vital capacity (FVC), and three studies assessed mid-peak expiratory flow (percent predicted). Six studies reported sputum weight as an outcome. Less frequently reported outcomes included oxygen saturation levels, personal preference, hospital admissions, use of intravenous antibiotics, and pseudomonas gene expression. No statistically significant differences were observed between autogenic drainage and other airway clearance techniques for the measured outcomes. However, in one study, participants expressed a preference for autogenic drainage over postural drainage and percussion. In conclusion, autogenic drainage is a demanding technique that requires dedication from the individual. While it has potential as an airway clearance method, the current evidence does not demonstrate its superiority over other techniques. Larger, well-designed studies are needed to better evaluate the effectiveness of autogenic drainage compared to other airway clearance methods. The small sample sizes and complex designs of the included studies, as well as the variability in study duration, made it challenging to perform a pooled analysis of the data.
